one_line: AI LABS team tests the Superpowers Claude Code plugin on a Trello-style app: enforced brainstorm, plan, subagent, TDD and review gates work, but they burn context fast and are best used selectively.
summary: The AI LABS team installs the Superpowers plugin for Claude Code and builds a Trello-like project management app with it. The plugin adds skills that run a fixed sequence: brainstorming with clarifying questions, three approaches, architecture and UX sign-off, a committed implementation plan, then subagent-driven implementation. Each subagent works in its own git worktree, and every task gets a spec-review subtask and a code-review skill before the next task starts. Test-first work is enforced through prompt cues that forbid editing tests. The speaker's main point is that this is enforcement with gates, not guidance like plan mode. The costs are heavy context use (about half the window for one iteration, with compaction needed after a few tasks), sequential execution, and the agent drifting back to native behavior when context runs low. The speakers conclude to use the full process only for tasks where Claude tends to fumble, and to let it work natively for small changes like UI tweaks.

key_ideas.idea: Superpowers is framed as enforcement, not guidance: each step has a gate and the agent cannot advance until the current step passes.
key_ideas.detail: Plain plan mode only guides the agent. The speaker says Superpowers blocks progress until the user approves or the step passes, which they argue is why it finishes the plan. Their reasoning covers the difference from plan mode and from BMAD/OpenSpec, which they say are spec-writing systems rather than workflow enforcement.

key_ideas.idea: Brainstorming skill replaces guessing with structured questions and sign-off before any code is written.
key_ideas.detail: For a vague app idea, the skill asks who the app is for, the tech stack, and the trade-offs of each choice. It flagged a browser-only database as a security/server-access problem, offered three approaches to pick from, then produced architecture and UX designs, confirmed the project structure, and saved the design docs to a docs folder. It also asked about small edge cases such as how empty columns should look.

key_ideas.idea: Planning is a committed artifact that splits the app into subtasks, and Git commits happen by default.
key_ideas.detail: The writing-plans skill produced an implementation plan and committed it. The speaker says the built-in Git commit discipline per change was the feature that other frameworks lacked and they had to enforce manually.

key_ideas.idea: Subagent-driven implementation uses one git worktree per subagent, with a spec review and code review gate for each task.
key_ideas.detail: The user picks subagent-driven implementation from two offered options. Each subagent gets its own worktree so parallel edits do not overwrite each other. After a task is committed, a separate subtask verifies it against the spec, then the code-reviewer skill checks quality. The next task starts only after approval. At the end the worktrees are removed and the work is merged into main.

key_ideas.idea: Context is the main cost: one iteration used roughly half the window, and a few tasks left about 5%.
key_ideas.detail: The subagents and multiple skills consume context quickly. The speakers ran the compact command before brainstorming the next feature so the earlier decisions were kept. They call for careful use of the process for this reason.

key_ideas.idea: Test-first is enforced by prompt cues that block test edits, which fixes a problem the speakers had with forced TDD.
key_ideas.detail: Subagents write tests for each part first, then implement until the tests pass without changing the tests. The skill text uses strong cues such as 'if there is even a 1% chance a skill applies, use it' to stop the agent from skipping steps. The trade-off is that the subagents run one task at a time, so the work is slower.

key_ideas.idea: Systematic debugging is a four-phase skill that works better than vague probing of the codebase.
key_ideas.detail: Given a vague bug report (data not saving on refresh), the skill runs: identify the root cause (asks the user questions, then traces the relevant files), isolate the bug, narrow down the actual reason, apply the fix, and finish with tests.

key_ideas.idea: Use the full process selectively; for small UI tweaks, plan with the skill and then implement natively.
key_ideas.detail: For a UI redesign that did not need the full 15-minute flow, the speakers asked for brainstorming and planning only, with no implementation. They then asked for implementation without the process. The changes still went into Git with the same commit format. The stated rule is to let Claude work natively where it is already good and bring in the process where it fumbles.

techniques.name: Install a workflow plugin from a marketplace in Claude Code
techniques.how: Copy the 'register marketplace' command the plugin's page gives, run it inside the Claude Code project, install the plugin from that marketplace, then restart Claude Code so the skills load. The exact command text is not shown in the transcript.
techniques.when: Adding Superpowers or a similar skill-based workflow plugin to a project that already uses Claude Code.

techniques.name: Brainstorm-gated kickoff prompt
techniques.how: Give a vague product request (the speakers used a Trello-like project management app). Let the brainstorming skill ask about users, stack, and trade-offs, pick one of the three approaches it offers, and approve the architecture and UX before it writes any docs or code.
techniques.when: Starting a new feature or app where the agent would otherwise guess at requirements or unstated details.

techniques.name: Subagent-driven implementation with worktrees and review gates
techniques.how: When the plan is ready, choose the subagent-driven option. Each task runs in its own git worktree. After the commit, a spec-check subtask runs, then the code-reviewer skill. Only then does the next task start. Merge into main and remove the worktrees at the end.
techniques.when: A multi-task build where parallel or sequential subagents must not overwrite each other, and each task needs a review before the next.

techniques.name: Anti-test-edit TDD cue
techniques.how: The skill tells subagents to write tests first, implement without touching the test files, and iterate until the tests pass. Strong 'if there is even a 1% chance a skill applies, use it' phrasing discourages skipping steps.
techniques.when: Enforcing red-green TDD with agents that otherwise edit tests to make them pass.

techniques.name: Four-phase systematic debugging prompt
techniques.how: Give a vague bug report and ask the agent to use systematic debugging. Expect it to ask for the symptoms, trace from there, isolate the bug, find the reason, fix it, and run tests.
techniques.when: Bugs where the agent would otherwise probe the codebase at random.

techniques.name: Compact before the next feature
techniques.how: Run the /compact command when a few tasks have used most of the context (about 5% left in the speakers' run), then start the next brainstorm.
techniques.when: Long multi-task sessions with heavy skill and subagent use, to keep the design decisions when the next brainstorm starts.

techniques.name: Selective process use
techniques.how: For small tasks, ask for brainstorming and planning only, stop before implementation, then ask Claude to implement the plan without the workflow. Keep the same commit format.
techniques.when: Small or cosmetic changes that do not justify the full process cost.

techniques.name: Re-invoke skills after context loss
techniques.how: If the agent reverts to native behavior when context is tight, remind it to use the plugin's skills by name.
techniques.when: Mid-session drift where the agent stops following the workflow.

numbers.claim: The Superpowers plugin reached about 58,000 GitHub stars in 24 hours (popularity, not a quality measure).
One iteration of the Superpowers process used almost 50% of the context window.
After a few tasks, only about 5% of context was left, so the team ran /compact before the next brainstorm.
Subagent TDD ran one task at a time, which the speakers say made it slower than native Claude Code (no timing given).

hot_takes: The title 'Fixed 90% of AI Coding Errors' overstates a single anecdotal run on one small Trello-style app. The video gives no error-rate measurement.
The main useful claim is that gates (not plan mode) keep the agent on track. This is a team's experience, not a benchmark.
The process spends a lot of context and runs sequentially, so it is a poor fit for every task. The speakers' own advice is to use it only where Claude tends to fail.
Mid-video plug for the AI LABS Pro community and a super-thanks ask. This is a channel plug, not a product sponsorship, and does not cap quality by itself.

relevance.why: Enforced step gates plus per-task spec and code review map onto checkpointed agent runs. The worktree-per-subagent pattern is relevant to parallel agent isolation. The context-cost numbers are useful for planning budgets.
relevance.action: Try a per-subagent git worktree plus a spec-review gate in one AgentOS agent run, and log context use per task to see whether the ~50%-per-iteration cost holds.

relevance.why: ProsHarness wraps Claude Code with plan, critique and debate, and checkpointed runs. Superpowers' brainstorm, plan commit, subagent review gates and compaction timing are close to that design and are a concrete comparison point.
relevance.action: Compare ProsHarness's plan, critique and debate gates with Superpowers' brainstorm, plan, spec-review and code-review gates, and try a spec-review step as a ProsHarness gate with a compaction trigger.
